steps.title: Look at the comparisons.
steps.why: Long adjectives take more instead of -er.
steps.html:
The nights are colder than the days.

Cairo's population is bigger than Sydney's.

Tokyo is more expensive than Singapore.

The South Pole is colder than the North Pole.

steps.title: Comparative adjectives
steps.html:
The adjectiveRuleExample
short (cold, small)+ -ercolder than
ends in -e (nice)+ -rnicer than
one vowel + consonant (big, hot)double + -erbigger than, hotter than
ends in -y (dry, busy)-y → -ierdrier than, busier than
long (expensive, beautiful)more + adjectivemore expensive than
irregular—good → better, bad → worse, far → further

The word after the comparison is always than.

To say two things are the same, use as … as: Today is as cold as yesterday.

Learners often write more colder. Use -er or more, never both.

steps.title: You are going to read about the weather then and now.
steps.sub: Do you think winters where you live are colder or warmer than before?

steps.title: 1 · Karaganda, then
steps.html:
My grandmother remembers the winters of the 1970s. The nights were colder than anything we know now — minus forty was normal, and the snow arrived in October and stayed until April.

Summers were shorter and drier. There were fewer storms, and the air in the town was worse: everybody used coal. She says the sky was greyer, but the winters were whiter.

steps.title: 2 · Karaganda, now
steps.html:
Today the winters are warmer and much shorter. The first snow comes in November and it is often gone by March. Minus forty is now unusual, and minus twenty feels cold.

The summers are hotter and wetter than they were. There are more storms and the temperature is higher, but the air is cleaner than in my grandmother's time. So is the weather better now? It is easier, but she says it is less beautiful.
